title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
summary: The solar system is organized around the Sun, with four small rocky planets, a belt of asteroids, and four giant gas planets spread across a vast distance.
poll: The Sun is the most important part of the solar system.

versions.title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
versions.text:
The solar system is the Sun's family. The Sun sits in the middle.

Look up at night. You may see bright dots. Some are stars. One big light is the Sun.

Eight worlds move around the Sun. We call them planets. This path is an orbit. Earth is one of them.

Four worlds are small and rocky. They are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. You could stand on them.

Past Mars is a belt of rocks. People call it a rock belt.

Then come four giant worlds. They are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. They are made of gas. You could not stand on them.

The Sun is huge. It gives light and heat to all. Its pull keeps each world on its path.

versions.title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
versions.text:
The solar system is the Sun's family of planets. The Sun sits at the middle.

Look up at the sky at night. You may see many bright dots. Some of those dots are stars, far away. One huge ball of light near us is the Sun.

Eight planets move around the Sun. This path is called an orbit. Earth is one of these planets.

The four planets near the Sun are small and rocky. They are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. You would feel hard ground.

Farther out, past Mars, lies a belt of rocks. We call it the rock belt.

Then come four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. These giants are made mostly of gas, not rock. There is no hard ground to stand on.

The Sun is huge next to the planets. It gives off light and heat to every planet. Its pull keeps them moving.

versions.title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
versions.text:
The solar system is the Sun's whole family of planets. They all move around one bright star.

Look up at the sky on a clear night. You may notice many bright dots. Some of those dots are stars, far away in space. One huge ball of light near us is the Sun.

Eight planets travel around the Sun along curved paths. Each path is an orbit. Earth is one of these planets.

The four planets closest to the Sun are fairly small and rocky. They are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. You would feel hard, rocky ground.

Farther out, past Mars, lies a wide belt of rock and metal. We call this the rock belt.

Then come four much bigger planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. These giants are made mostly of gas and ice. There is no hard ground to stand on.

The Sun itself is huge. It holds almost all of the system's stuff inside it. Its strong pull keeps every planet moving on its path.

versions.title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
versions.text:
The solar system is the Sun's whole family of planets. They all move around one bright, central star.

Look up at the sky on a clear night. You may notice countless bright dots scattered across the dark. Many of those dots are distant stars, far beyond our own neighborhood. One huge ball of light near us is the Sun.

Eight planets travel around the Sun along curved paths called orbits. Earth is one of these eight planets. Together, the Sun and its planets make up the solar system.

The four planets closest to the Sun are fairly small and rocky. In order, they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars. You would feel hard, rocky ground.

Farther out, past Mars, lies a wide belt of rock and metal, left over from long ago. We call this the rock belt. It marks a boundary between the rocky planets and what comes next.

Then come four much bigger planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. These giants are made mostly of gas and ice, not rock. There is no hard ground where anyone could stand.

The Sun itself is so huge that it holds almost all of the system's material inside it. Light from the Sun takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. The Sun's pull keeps every planet moving on its path.

versions.title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
versions.text:
On a clear night, the sky fills with points of light. Most are distant stars far beyond our own corner of space. One brilliant ball of light much closer to us is the Sun, the star that anchors our solar system.

Eight planets orbit the Sun, held in place by the Sun's gravity. Gravity is the invisible force that pulls objects toward each other. Earth is the third planet from the Sun. It follows Mercury and Venus, and is followed by Mars.

These four inner worlds, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are called terrestrial planets. Like Earth, they have solid, rocky surfaces. They are also fairly small compared to what lies farther out.

Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt, a wide region packed with leftover rock and metal from the system's early history. The belt roughly marks the boundary between the rocky planets and the larger worlds beyond it.

Past the belt orbit four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. Unlike the terrestrial planets, these giants have no solid surface. They are built mostly from thick layers of gas and ice.

The distance across the solar system is hard to imagine. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. It takes more than four hours to reach distant Neptune, showing just how vast the system truly is.

versions.title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
versions.text:
On a clear night, the sky fills with countless points of light, most of them distant stars far beyond our own corner of space. One brilliant ball of light much closer to us, however, is the Sun, the star that so thoroughly dominates our solar system that it holds more than 99 percent of the system's total mass.

Eight planets orbit the Sun along elliptical paths, meaning each orbit is a slightly stretched circle rather than a perfect one. They are held in place by the Sun's gravity, the force that pulls every object with mass toward every other object with mass. Earth is the third planet from the Sun, following Mercury and Venus, and followed by Mars.

These four inner worlds, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are called terrestrial planets because, like Earth, each has a solid, rocky surface and a composition dominated by rock and metal rather than gas. They are fairly small and close together compared with the larger worlds farther out.

Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt, a region packed with leftover chunks of rock and metal from the system's early formation, more than four billion years ago. The belt roughly marks the boundary between the rocky planets and the larger worlds beyond it.

Past the belt orbit four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, whose composition is dominated by gas and ice rather than solid rock, leaving them with no true surface at all.

Beyond Neptune lies an even more distant zone called the Kuiper Belt, home to small, icy worlds such as Pluto. These distant bodies are usually called dwarf planets rather than full planets, since they are smaller and share their orbital neighborhood with many other icy objects. They still travel around the Sun, though far more slowly than Neptune does, because they orbit so much farther away.

The vast scale of the solar system is almost impossible to grasp. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, yet more than four hours to reach distant Neptune, a vivid reminder of just how vast the system truly is.

One brilliant ball of light much closer to us, however, is the Sun, the star that so thoroughly dominates our solar system that it alone holds more than 99 percent of the system's total mass, dwarfing every planet combined.

Eight planets orbit the Sun along elliptical paths, meaning each orbit traces a slightly stretched circle rather than a perfect one. They are held firmly in place by the Sun's gravity, the force that pulls every object with mass toward every other object with mass, regardless of how far apart they happen to be. Earth is the third planet from the Sun, following Mercury and Venus, and followed by Mars, before the asteroid belt and the four outer giants begin their procession.

These four inner worlds, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are called terrestrial planets because, like Earth, each has a solid, rocky surface and a composition dominated by rock and metal rather than gas or ice. They are fairly small and close together, at least by the standards of the much larger worlds that lie farther out.

Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt, a region packed with countless leftover chunks of rock and metal left over from the system's early formation, more than four billion years ago, when the planets themselves were still gradually taking shape. The belt roughly marks the boundary between the rocky planets and the larger worlds beyond it.

Past the belt orbit four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, whose composition is dominated by gas and ice rather than solid rock, leaving them with no true surface where anything could ever land or stand safely.

Beyond Neptune lies an even more distant zone called the Kuiper Belt, home to small, icy worlds such as Pluto. These distant bodies are usually classified as dwarf planets rather than full planets, since they are considerably smaller and share their orbital neighborhood with countless other icy objects drifting through the same remote region. They still travel around the Sun in long, slow orbits, though far more slowly than Neptune does, simply because they circle so much farther away from the Sun's gravitational pull.

The vast scale of the solar system is almost impossible to grasp using everyday measurements. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, yet more than four hours to reach distant Neptune, a vivid and humbling reminder of just how vast the system truly is.

versions.title: The Solar System: A Family of Planets
versions.text:
On a clear night, the sky fills with countless points of light, the overwhelming majority of them distant stars lying far beyond our own corner of space entirely, scattered across galaxies that the unaided eye can barely begin to resolve. One brilliant ball of light much closer to us, however, is the Sun, the star that anchors our entire solar system and so thoroughly dominates it that it alone accounts for more than 99 percent of the system's total mass, dwarfing every planet combined many times over.

Eight planets orbit the Sun along elliptical paths, meaning each orbit traces a slightly stretched circle rather than a perfect one, held firmly in place by the Sun's gravity, the invisible force that pulls every object with mass toward every other object with mass, regardless of how far apart they happen to be. Earth is the third planet from the Sun, following Mercury and Venus, and followed in turn by Mars, before the asteroid belt and the four outer giants begin their own stately procession around the Sun.

These four inner worlds, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, are called terrestrial planets because, like Earth, each one has a solid, rocky surface and a composition dominated overwhelmingly by rock and metal rather than gas or ice. They are also fairly small and relatively close together, at least by the standards of the much larger worlds that lie farther out in the system.

Beyond Mars lies the asteroid belt, a wide region packed with countless leftover chunks of rock and metal left over from the solar system's early formation, more than four billion years ago, when the planets themselves were still gradually taking shape from a swirling disk of dust and gas. The asteroid belt roughly marks the boundary between the small rocky planets and the much larger worlds that orbit beyond it.

Past the asteroid belt orbit four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, whose composition is dominated by gas and ice rather than solid rock, leaving them with no true surface where anything could ever land or stand safely.

The vast scale of the solar system is almost impossible to grasp using everyday measurements. Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth, yet it takes more than four hours to reach distant Neptune, and objects far beyond Neptune take even longer still, a vivid and humbling reminder of just how vast the whole system truly is, and how small our own planet remains within it.

MID.prompt: Explain how the asteroid belt divides the solar system into two groups of planets. Use evidence from the article.
checklist: I explained what the asteroid belt divides.
I named both groups of planets.
I used evidence from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: The asteroid belt sits between Mars and Jupiter, and it roughly marks the boundary between the two main groups of planets. On the inner side are the four terrestrial planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars, which have solid, rocky surfaces. On the outer side are the four giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, which are made mostly of gas and ice with no solid surface at all. The asteroid belt itself is made of leftover rock and metal from the solar system's early formation, so it clearly separates the small rocky worlds from the much larger gas giants.

HIGH.prompt: The article says the Sun 'dominates' the solar system. Explain what this means and support your answer with at least two pieces of evidence.
checklist: I explained what it means for the Sun to dominate the solar system.
I gave at least two pieces of evidence.
I connected the evidence to my explanation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: When the article says the Sun dominates the solar system, it means the Sun is by far the largest and most powerful part of it. One piece of evidence is that the Sun holds more than 99 percent of the entire solar system's mass, dwarfing every planet combined. A second piece of evidence is that the Sun's gravity controls the elliptical orbits of all eight planets, keeping them moving along their paths no matter how vast the distance separating them. Together, this enormous mass and controlling gravity show why the Sun, rather than any planet, truly dominates the whole system.
